2.text: person has hurt his foot with an axe, or has severed a vein, so that blood

3.text: spurts out like a jet of urine, it is a cause of great fright. If the flow of

4.text: blood is not stopped right away, it will cause death. I have an incantation

5.text: for such an occasion. One must demand help from the Zenith. The person

6.text: says, “Come down, you flying spider, who are the Spider of the Time of the

7.text: First Creation.” Then he appears to be taking the spider in his left hand.

8.text: “There, now! sew this together.” He appears to sew the wound, and then

9.text: bandages it with scraps of skin. When, after some time, the bandages are

10.text: undone, the cut is closed and looks quite like an old scar.¹

11.text: (j) For curing a Swelling. To reduce a swelling which is slow in

12.text: bursting, I have a special incantation. I say, “There is a Little Seal of the

13.text: Time of the First Creation. I have transformed myself into that seal, and I

14.text: have pierced the thick ice above!” Then I breathe three times over the

15.text: swelling, which bursts after a while, or perhaps on the next day.²

16.text: (i) and (j) told by a Reindeer Chukchee of the Kolyma Country.

17.text: (k) Another Cure for a Swelling. Inside of the swelling there lies a

18.text: boneless fish, — a Sturgeon. He moves his sharp fins, and cuts up the

19.text: swelled place. On the top of the swelling there lies a Hare. He makes the

20.text: snow under him melt with warmth. Between the two, the swelling bursts.

21.text: Told by Hɪyewteˊhɪn (man) at Mariinsky Post, 1900.

22.text: (l) For curing an Ailing Limb. Taking a piece of cloth, I go out of the

23.text: house early in the morning, and, turning to the Dawn, say, “O Dawn! this

24.text: is my sea. Give upon my sea a wing of the butterfly.” With this wing I

25.text: rub the patient. This is not an ailing limb; this is the ground. I rub it

26.text: with the wing from the upper earth of the Dawn, then it will stop ailing.

27.text: Told by Scratching-Woman (man) at Mariinsky Post, 1900.

28.text: (m) For curing Pain in the Legs. This is not a leg; it is a place

29.text: chosen by the Raven for its night’s repose. The Mouse-Woman and the

30.text: Spermophilus-Woman scrape off the snow. The Raven asks of his wives,

31.text: “Why is that stranger suffering so from pain in his leg?” — “We do not

32.text: know.” The Raven goes to the Pebbly River. “I will bring some of its

33.text: water, and I will rub it over the ailing place: let it cease to feel pain.”

34.text: Then he goes away to the Northeast Wind. “Halloo!” — “Halloo!” — “Why

35.text: is this stranger suffering so from his leg? I could not do anything. My

36.text: single incantation was spoiled by my own wife!” — “Well, go home!” After

37.text: a while there comes the Northeast Wind, which carries away the fallen leaves

38.text: and the rubbish, and thoroughly cleans the ailing spot.

39.text: Told by Hɪyewteˊhɪn (man) at Mariinsky Post, 1900.
